subject: Mathematics

unit.unitOverview: Welcome to Unit 7. In this unit you will master fractions – one of the most important and most useful ideas in all of mathematics. A fraction is simply a way of describing a part of a whole, or a part of a group. You already meet fractions every single day, even when you do not name them. When Amina divides a warm anjero into equal pieces to share at breakfast, when Yusuf notices that Asr is about three-quarters of the way through the afternoon, or when Halima weighs out half a kilogram of dates at the Hargeisa market, they are all thinking in fractions.
learningPath: Preview the goals and core ideas
Learn methods and study worked examples
Complete guided practice, activities and games
Apply, explain and complete the Unit Challenge

objectives.text: Estimate, multiply and divide decimals by whole numbers.
Estimate, multiply and divide proper fractions.
Understand lowest common multiple and highest common factor (numbers less than 100).
Understand the relative size of quantities to compare and order decimals and fractions, using the symbols =, ≠, > and <.
Understand how ratios are used to compare quantities to divide an amount into a given ratio with two parts.
Estimate and add mixed numbers, and write the answer as a mixed number in its simplest form.

outcomes: Recognise proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers, and explain the difference.
Find equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number.
Simplify a fraction to its lowest terms using the highest common factor.
Compare and order fractions using common denominators, cross-multiplication and decimals.
Add and subtract fractions with the same and with different denominators, including mixed numbers.
Multiply fractions, whole numbers and mixed numbers, cancelling where possible.
Divide fractions using the reciprocal (‘multiply by the flip’) method.

concepts.title: Understanding Fractions and Their Types
concepts.explanation:
A fraction describes a part of a whole or a part of a group. It is written as two numbers separated by a line. The numerator on top tells you how many parts you have. The denominator on the bottom tells you how many equal parts the whole has been divided into. The word *equal* is the key – the parts must be the same size for the fraction to make sense.

Picture a large sambusa platter cut into 8 equal pieces for iftar. If Hassan takes 3 pieces, he has taken 3/8 of the platter. The denominator, 8, tells us the platter was cut into eight equal pieces; the numerator, 3, tells us how many of those pieces were taken. Change the size of the pieces and you change the denominator; change how many you take and you change the numerator.

Fractions appear everywhere once you start to look. 45 minutes is 3/4 of an hour, because an hour has 60 minutes and 45 is three of the four quarters. 25 shillings out of every 100 is 1/4 of a shilling-hundred. Winning 3 out of 5 football matches is a 3/5 success rate. In each case a whole is split into equal parts and we count how many of those parts we mean.

There are three types of fraction you must recognise instantly:

Proper fractions have a numerator smaller than the denominator, such as 3/4, 2/5 and 7/8. Their value is always between 0 and 1 – they are less than one whole.

Improper fractions have a numerator equal to or larger than the denominator, such as 5/4, 7/3 and 9/9. Their value is always 1 or more – they are one whole or more. (An improper fraction is sometimes called a ‘top-heavy’ fraction.)

Mixed numbers combine a whole number with a proper fraction, such as 2 1/3 and 5 2/7. They express the same quantity as an improper fraction but in a form that is often easier to picture.
concepts.example: Notice that improper fractions and mixed numbers are two ways of writing the *same* amount when that amount is more than one whole. The improper fraction 7/3 and the mixed number 2 1/3 sit on exactly the same point on the number line. You will learn to switch between the two forms in Concept 7, and you will choose whichever form makes a calculation easier.

concepts.title: Equivalent Fractions and Simplifying
concepts.explanation:
Equivalent fractions look different but have exactly the same value. They mark the same point on the number line and describe the same amount of a whole. For example, 1/2, 2/4, 3/6, 4/8 and 5/10 are all equivalent – each one is exactly half. If you cut an anjero into 2 pieces and take 1, or cut it into 8 pieces and take 4, you have taken the same amount of bread.

You create an equivalent fraction by multiplying the numerator and denominator by the same number. Because you are multiplying the top and bottom by the same thing, you are really multiplying by 1 in disguise, so the value does not change. For example, 2/3 × 4/4 = 8/12, and 3/4 × 5/5 = 15/20. The fraction looks bigger but is worth the same.

Going the other way, you simplify (or reduce) a fraction by dividing the numerator and denominator by the same number. A fraction is in its lowest terms when the only number that divides into both top and bottom is 1. To simplify in a single step, divide both parts by their highest common factor (HCF) – the largest number that goes into both.

Let us simplify 12/18. First list the factors. Factors of 12: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 12. Factors of 18: 1, 2, 3, 6, 9, 18. The largest factor in both lists is 6, so the HCF is 6. Now divide: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3, giving 2/3. Since 2 and 3 share no factor except 1, the fraction 2/3 is fully simplified.
concepts.example: You do not have to find the HCF in one go. You may simplify in several smaller steps and still reach the same answer. For 12/18 you could divide top and bottom by 2 to get 6/9, then divide by 3 to get 2/3. Both routes arrive at the same lowest-terms fraction, so use whichever is easier for you. Always check your final answer really is fully simplified.

concepts.title: Comparing and Ordering Fractions
concepts.explanation: To compare two fractions is to decide which is greater, which is smaller, or whether they are equal. You cannot simply look at the numbers, because a bigger denominator does not mean a bigger fraction – in fact, for the same numerator, a bigger denominator means smaller pieces. There are three reliable methods, and you should know all three. Rewrite both fractions as equivalent fractions with the same denominator, then compare the numerators. Compare 3/4 and 5/6. The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12, so use 12 as the common denominator: 3/4 becomes 9/12 and 5/6 becomes 10/12, so 5/6 is the greater fraction.
concepts.example: For fractions a/b and c/d, compare the products a × d and b × c. If a × d is larger, then a/b is larger. Compare 2/3 and 3/5: 2 × 5 = 10 and 3 × 3 = 9. Since 10 > 9, we have 2/3 > 3/5. This is really the common-denominator method done quickly, because you are comparing the numerators you would get after making the denominators match.

concepts.title: Adding and Subtracting Fractions
concepts.explanation:
You can only add or subtract fractions when the pieces are the same size – that is, when the denominators match. This is just like coins: you cannot directly add a handful of 5-shilling pieces to a handful of 10-shilling pieces until you express them in the same unit. The denominator is the ‘unit’ of a fraction, so it must be common before you combine.

When the denominators are already equal, add or subtract the numerators and keep the denominator the same. The rule is a/c + b/c = (a + b)/c. For example, 2/7 + 3/7 = 5/7, and 5/9 − 2/9 = 3/9 = 1/3 after simplifying. If Amina eats 2/8 of a platter at lunch and 3/8 at dinner, she has eaten 2/8 + 3/8 = 5/8 in total. Always check whether your answer can be simplified.

When the denominators differ, first find a common denominator – usually the LCM of the two denominators – then rewrite each fraction with that denominator, then add or subtract the numerators, and finally simplify. Follow these steps:

Convert each fraction to an equivalent fraction over that common denominator.

Add or subtract the numerators; keep the common denominator.

Example: 1/4 + 1/6. The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. Convert: 1/4 = 3/12 and 1/6 = 2/12. Add: 3/12 + 2/12 = 5/12, which is already in lowest terms. Example: 5/6 − 1/4. The LCM of 6 and 4 is 12, so 5/6 = 10/12 and 1/4 = 3/12, giving 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12.

There are two good methods for mixed numbers. Method A turns each mixed number into an improper fraction, then adds or subtracts as usual. For 2 1/3 + 1 1/4: change to 7/3 and 5/4; the LCM of 3 and 4 is 12, so 7/3 = 28/12 and 5/4 = 15/12; then 28/12 + 15/12 = 43/12 = 3 7/12. Method B deals with the whole numbers and the fraction parts separately. For 3 2/5 + 2 1/3: add the wholes, 3 + 2 = 5; add the fractions, 2/5 + 1/3 = 6/15 + 5/15 = 11/15; combine to get 5 11/15.
concepts.example: Subtraction of mixed numbers sometimes needs borrowing, just like column subtraction with whole numbers. If the first fraction part is smaller than the second, borrow one whole from the whole-number part and add it to the fraction. Example: 4 1/6 − 2 2/3. Write 2/3 as 4/6. Since 1/6 is smaller than 4/6, borrow: 4 1/6 becomes 3 7/6 (we took one whole, worth 6/6, and added it to 1/6). Now subtract: 3 7/6 − 2 4/6 = 1 3/6 = 1 1/2.

concepts.title: Multiplying Fractions
concepts.explanation:
Multiplying fractions is often easier than adding them, because you do not need a common denominator. The rule is simple: multiply the numerators together, and multiply the denominators together. In symbols, a/b × c/d = (a × c)/(b × d). For example, 2/3 × 1/4 = 2/12 = 1/6, and 3/5 × 2/7 = 6/35.

The word ‘of’ is the key to understanding fraction multiplication. When you work out 1/2 × 3/4 you are finding 1/2 of 3/4 – half of three-quarters. Taking a fraction of a fraction always gives a smaller result, which is why multiplying two proper fractions gives an answer smaller than either one. This surprises many learners at first, but it makes sense: half of a small thing is smaller still.

You can make the numbers smaller – and avoid heavy simplifying at the end – by cancelling common factors before multiplying. Example: 4/9 × 3/8. Here 4 and 8 share a factor of 4, so cancel them to 1 and 2; the 9 and 3 share a factor of 3, so cancel to 3 and 1. This leaves 1/3 × 1/2 = 1/6. Cancelling early keeps the arithmetic light and is a mark of confident work.

Any whole number can be written as a fraction over 1. So 3 × 2/5 = 3/1 × 2/5 = 6/5 = 1 1/5. For mixed numbers, first convert to improper fractions, then multiply. Example: 2 1/3 × 1 1/2 = 7/3 × 3/2 = 21/6 = 3 1/2. Never multiply the whole-number parts and fraction parts separately – that is a very common error. Always convert to improper fractions first.
concepts.example: Multiplication is exactly how you find a fraction of an amount, which you will meet fully in Concept 8. For now, notice that 3/4 of 20 is 3/4 × 20 = 15, and 2/5 of 35 is 2/5 × 35 = 14. Multiplication also appears in area (a rug 2/3 m by 3/4 m has area 3/4 × 2/3 = 1/2 square metre) and in probability (if independent events have probabilities 1/3 and 1/4, both happening has probability 1/3 × 1/4 = 1/12).

concepts.title: Dividing Fractions
concepts.explanation:
Why does flipping work? Think about the question ‘how many 1/4s are in 3/4?’ That is exactly 3/4 ÷ 1/4, and the answer is 3, because three quarter-pieces make three-quarters. Dividing tells you how many of the smaller piece fit inside the larger amount, and multiplying by the reciprocal counts them for you.

The reciprocal is found by swapping numerator and denominator: the reciprocal of 3/4 is 4/3, the reciprocal of 2/5 is 5/2, and the reciprocal of a whole number 7 (that is, 7/1) is 1/7. Now work some examples:

3/4 ÷ 1/2 = 3/4 × 2/1 = 6/4 = 3/2 = 1 1/2.

2/3 ÷ 4/5 = 2/3 × 5/4 = 10/12 = 5/6.

5/6 ÷ 2/3 = 5/6 × 3/2 = 15/12 = 1 1/4.

Dividing by a whole number: write the whole number over 1 and flip it. So 3/4 ÷ 3 = 3/4 × 1/3 = 3/12 = 1/4. Dividing a whole number by a fraction: 6 ÷ 2/3 = 6/1 × 3/2 = 18/2 = 9. That last answer makes sense: if you share 6 into groups each of size 2/3, you get 9 groups.
concepts.example: Mixed numbers must be converted to improper fractions before you divide. Example: 2 1/2 ÷ 1 1/4 = 5/2 ÷ 5/4 = 5/2 × 4/5 = 20/10 = 2. And 4 2/3 ÷ 2 = 14/3 ÷ 2/1 = 14/3 × 1/2 = 14/6 = 7/3 = 2 1/3. The single most common division mistake is flipping the wrong fraction – always flip the one you are dividing by (the second one), never the first.

methods.title: How to add or subtract fractions
steps: Find the LCM of the denominators.
Rewrite each fraction over that common denominator.
Add or subtract the numerators; keep the denominator.
Simplify the answer.

methods.title: How to divide fractions
steps: Convert any whole or mixed numbers to improper fractions.
Keep the first fraction as it is.
Change ÷ to × and flip the second fraction (its reciprocal).
Multiply, then simplify.

methods.title: How to find a fraction of an amount
steps: Divide the amount by the denominator.
Multiply the result by the numerator.
Check the answer is sensible (a proper fraction of an amount is smaller than the amount).

methods.title: How to convert a mixed number to an improper fraction
steps: Multiply the whole number by the denominator.
Add the numerator.
Write the result over the original denominator.

methods.title: Multiply with cancelling
steps: Cancel first.
6 and 15 share a factor of 3, becoming 2 and 5.
Then 14 and 7 share a factor of 7, becoming 2 and 1.
This leaves 2/1 × 2/5 = 4/5.

methods.title: Divide fractions
steps: Convert the mixed number: 2 1/4 = 9/4.
Keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, and flip the second fraction upside down.
Check by multiplying your answer by 3/4 — it should give back 9/4.

workedExamples.title: Simplify a fraction
workedExamples.solution: The HCF of 18 and 24 is 6. Divide both parts by 6: 18 ÷ 6 = 3 and 24 ÷ 6 = 4. So 18/24 = 3/4. Check: 3 and 4 share no factor except 1, so it is fully simplified.

workedExamples.title: Compare two fractions
workedExamples.solution: Use a common denominator. The LCM of 8 and 3 is 24. Convert: 5/8 = 15/24 and 2/3 = 16/24. Since 16 > 15, 2/3 > 5/8.

workedExamples.title: Add fractions with different denominators
workedExamples.solution: The LCM of 4 and 6 is 12. Convert: 3/4 = 9/12 and 1/6 = 2/12. Add the numerators: 9/12 + 2/12 = 11/12. It is already in lowest terms.

workedExamples.title: Subtract mixed numbers with borrowing
workedExamples.solution: The fraction part 1/4 is smaller than 3/4, so borrow one whole from the 4: 4 1/4 = 3 5/4. Now subtract: 3 5/4 − 2 3/4 = 1 2/4 = 1 1/2.

workedExamples.title: Multiply with cancelling
workedExamples.solution: Cancel first. 6 and 15 share a factor of 3, becoming 2 and 5. Then 14 and 7 share a factor of 7, becoming 2 and 1. This leaves 2/1 × 2/5 = 4/5. So the answer is 4/5.

workedExamples.title: Divide fractions
workedExamples.solution: Convert the mixed number: 2 1/4 = 9/4. Keep, change, flip: 9/4 ÷ 3/4 = 9/4 × 4/3 = 36/12 = 3.

workedExamples.title: Fraction of an amount
workedExamples.solution: Divide by the denominator, then multiply by the numerator. 32 ÷ 8 = 4, then 4 × 3 = 12.

workedExamples.title: A backwards problem
workedExamples.prompt: If 2/5 of a number is 12, what is the number?
workedExamples.solution: If 2/5 is 12, then 1/5 is 12 ÷ 2 = 6. The whole is five fifths, so 5 × 6 = 30. Check: 2/5 of 30 = 12. ✓

activities.title: Fraction Strips from Paper
activities.materials: several strips of paper the same length, a pencil, a ruler.
steps: Leave one strip whole – this is 1.
Fold a second strip into 2 equal parts and label each 1/2. Fold others into 3, 4, 6 and 8 equal parts.
Line the strips up. Which fractions are equal? (Look for 1/2 = 2/4 = 3/6 = 4/8.)
Use the strips to show that 1/2 is bigger than 1/3, even though 3 is bigger than 2. Explain why in your own words.
Keep your fraction strips – they are a model you can use all through this unit.

activities.title: Recipe Scaling in the Kitchen
activities.materials: a simple recipe (for anjero, bariis or a cake) with fractional amounts.
steps: Write down each ingredient amount as a fraction or mixed number.
Halve the recipe: multiply every amount by 1/2. Record the new amounts.
Double the recipe: multiply every amount by 2. Record these too.
Explain to a family member — or your AI tutor if none is available — why 1/2 of 2 1/4 cups is 1 1/8 cups.

activities.title: The Fraction War Card Game
activities.materials: paper cards, each with a fraction written on it (mix easy and hard, such as 1/2, 2/3, 3/4, 5/8, 7/12).
steps: Shuffle the cards and deal them equally between two players. If you are working alone, deal two hands and play both, or ask your AI tutor to be your opponent.
Each player turns over one card at the same time.
Whoever has the larger fraction wins both cards – prove it using a common denominator.
Play until one player holds all the cards. Keep a note of any comparison that was hard.
This game trains you to compare fractions quickly and to justify your answer.

activities.title: Fractions of Amounts Market Stall
activities.materials: small objects to be ‘goods’ (dates, stones as shillings), and paper price labels.
steps: Set out a pile of, say, 24 dates. Ask a partner — or your AI tutor if working alone — to find 3/4 of them, then 1/3, then 5/8.
Announce a ‘1/4 off’ sale: work out the new price of a 60-shilling item.
Set a backwards puzzle: ‘2/5 of my dates is 8. How many did I start with?’
Swap roles and check each other’s working, or check your own working against the answers if working alone.

activities.title: Design a Fraction Wall (Investigation)
activities.materials: a large sheet of paper, a ruler, coloured pencils.
steps: Draw a rectangle and split it into 1 whole, then rows of 2, 3, 4, 6, 8 and 12 equal parts.
Colour each row and label every part with its fraction.
Use the wall to find as many equivalent fractions as you can – line up the edges.
Investigate: which fractions on your wall can be simplified, and to what?

activities.title: Family Fraction Challenge
activities.materials: your family or friends (or your AI tutor if working alone), paper and pencil.
steps: Each person (or you and your AI tutor) writes three fraction questions (one add, one multiply, one ‘fraction of an amount’).
Swap papers and solve. Show full working.
Mark each other’s answers and talk through any disagreements.
Award a point for each correct, fully simplified answer. Highest score wins.

After your activities, talk or write about: Which activity helped you understand fractions best? What was the trickiest part – comparing, simplifying, or dividing? What would you like more practice with? Share your answers with your teacher at your next session.

rules.title: Key rule 1
rules.text: Equivalent and Simplifying Multiply top and bottom by the same number to make an equivalent fraction. Divide top and bottom by their highest common factor to simplify. Lowest terms: the only common factor left is 1.

rules.title: Add and Subtract Rule
rules.text: Make the denominators the same (use the LCM), then add or subtract the numerators. Keep the common denominator; never add the denominators. Simplify the answer at the end.

rules.title: Multiply Rule
rules.text: Multiply the numerators, multiply the denominators. Cancel common factors before multiplying to keep numbers small. Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first.

rules.title: Divide Rule
rules.text: Keep, change, flip: keep the first, change divide to multiply, flip the second. Only flip the fraction you are dividing by. Convert mixed numbers to improper fractions first.

reasoningPrompts.prompt: If 3/4 of a number is 21, what is the number? Show your method.
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 28 (one quarter is 21 ÷ 3 = 7, so the whole is 4 × 7 = 28).

reasoningPrompts.prompt: If 2/7 of a class is 8 students, how many students are in the class?
reasoningPrompts.modelAnswer: 28 students (one seventh of the class is 8 ÷ 2 = 4, so the whole class is 7 × 4 = 28).

questions.question: Which of these is an improper fraction?
questions.hint: Compare the numerator and the denominator.
questions.explanation: An improper fraction has a numerator that is equal to or greater than its denominator. In 9/5 the numerator (9) is greater than the denominator (5), so it is improper. The other fractions all have a smaller numerator than denominator, so they are proper fractions.

questions.question: Which fraction is equivalent to 2/3?
questions.hint: Multiply the numerator and denominator of 2/3 by the same number.
questions.explanation: Multiply top and bottom of 2/3 by 2: 2 × 2 = 4 and 3 × 2 = 6, so 2/3 = 4/6.

questions.question: Simplify 12/18 to its lowest terms.
questions.hint: Find the highest common factor of 12 and 18.
questions.explanation: The HCF of 12 and 18 is 6. Divide both parts by 6: 12 ÷ 6 = 2 and 18 ÷ 6 = 3, so 12/18 = 2/3.

questions.question: Which fraction is larger: 1/2 or 1/4?
questions.hint: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
questions.explanation: Halves are bigger than quarters, so 1/2 is larger than 1/4.

questions.question: Work out 3/8 + 1/4.
questions.hint: Rewrite 1/4 with a denominator of 8 first.
questions.explanation: Convert to a common denominator: 1/4 = 2/8. Then 3/8 + 2/8 = 5/8.

questions.question: What is 1/5 of 50?
questions.hint: Work it out yourself first, then look for your answer among the options.

questions.question: Work out 3/5 ÷ 2/3.
questions.explanation: Keep the first fraction, change ÷ to ×, and flip the second fraction: 3/5 ÷ 2/3 = 3/5 × 3/2 = 9/10.

questions.question: Which fraction is equivalent to 1/2?
questions.hint: Estimate roughly what the answer should be, then pick the option closest to it.
questions.explanation: 2/4 simplifies to 1/2, so they are equivalent.

questions.question: Which of these is a mixed number?
questions.hint: Look for a whole number part plus a fraction part.
questions.explanation: A mixed number combines a whole number and a proper fraction, like 2 3/4. 11/4 is an improper fraction, and 5/8 and 7/7 are not mixed numbers.

selfAssessment: I can recognise proper fractions, improper fractions and mixed numbers, and explain the difference.
I can find equivalent fractions by multiplying or dividing numerator and denominator by the same number.
I can simplify a fraction to its lowest terms using the highest common factor.
I can compare and order fractions using common denominators, cross-multiplication and decimals.
I can add and subtract fractions with the same and with different denominators, including mixed numbers.
I can multiply fractions, whole numbers and mixed numbers, cancelling where possible.
I can divide fractions using the reciprocal (‘multiply by the flip’) method.
